title: Horizontal beam held by rope against a wall
what_it_asks: You are given a horizontal plank or beam touching or hinged to a wall. An inclined rope holds it up, and a load sits on it. You find the tension by taking moments, then the wall's reaction and its direction, and sometimes the range of positions where the load can safely go. The idea is that a body in equilibrium has zero net force and zero net turning effect.
typical_structure: Most questions have two parts, sometimes one or three. The first part is usually a moments calculation for the tension. A later part then resolves horizontally and vertically to get the wall reaction, its size and its angle. Some questions add a part with a limit on the tension or the load position, or a "show that" part. Marks per part are often 3 to 6, and later parts normally reuse the tension from earlier.
mark_pattern: The most typical part is three marks: M1 A1 A1. You earn the M1 for a moments equation about a sensible point with every relevant term present and the rope's force resolved correctly. Then come two accuracy marks: one for an equation that is right, and one for the final value of the tension. Longer parts run M1 A1 M1 A1 dM1 A1. There you write a moments equation, then a resolving equation, and finally combine the components for the size or angle of the reaction. That last method mark depends on the earlier ones. Some parts are a single B1 for a stated modelling fact. "Show that" parts end with a starred accuracy mark that needs a clean route to the printed value.

where_marks_leak.text: This is a common slip. You give the tension or reaction to the wrong number of significant figures, or with too many digits for the value of $g$ used. The final A1 is lost even though the method was sound.
You put a clockwise moment and an anticlockwise moment on the same side of the equation without a sign change. The moments M1 is lost, and the accuracy marks that depend on it go with it.
You round the tension early and use that value to find the wall reaction. The final A1 drifts out of range and is lost.
Your equation is set up correctly but a numerical error gives a wrong tension. The A1 is lost, though the method mark stays safe.
When you combine two equations for two unknowns, you add where you should subtract. The dependent method mark for solving is lost, and the accuracy mark after it.

write_to_earn: Mark the pivot point and write the moments equation in words or symbols before you put in any numbers.
Resolve the tension into its horizontal and vertical components with the angle shown clearly, then use the correct component in each moment.
Write the horizontal and vertical resolving equations as separate lines, with the wall's components labelled.
Keep unrounded values from the tension onward, and round only at the end to the accuracy the value of $g$ supports.
In a show-that part, write the line just before the printed result, then state the result.
